units.title: Acids, Bases and Salts
units.intro: Acid in water: source of H⁺ (H₃O⁺). Base: source of OH⁻ or a H⁺ acceptor. Alkali = soluble base. Strong = fully split; weak = partly split. That is not the same as concentrated.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which acidic ternary acid is formed when Sulfur Trioxide gas ($$\text{SO}_3$$) reacts with water?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write the chemical equation**
Reacting a nonmetallic oxide with water forms a ternary acid:
$$\text{SO}_3\text{(g)} + \text{H}_2\text{O(l)} \longrightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}$$

**Step 2: Identify the product name**
$$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$ is named **Sulfuric acid**.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct option is **Sulfuric acid ($$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$$)**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the characteristic color of the acid-base indicator phenolphthalein when added to a basic (alkaline) solution?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall indicator color transitions**
Phenolphthalein has a pH transition range of $$8.2 - 10.0$$.
*   In acidic solutions ($$\text{pH} < 7$$), it is **colorless**.
*   In basic solutions ($$\text{pH} > 7$$), it turns **bright pink**.

**Step 2: Final Answer**
The correct color in base is **Bright Pink**.

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: They are either weak acids or weak bases.
options.B: They demonstrate the end point of acid-base reactions.
options.C: The color of Phenolphthalein in an acidic solution is pink.
options.D: They change color either by losing or gaining H+ ions.

cards.why: Option C is incorrect because **Phenolphthalein is colorless** in acidic solutions. It turns **pink/magenta** in basic (alkaline) solutions. All other statements are correct descriptions of indicators.

cards.title: Step by step: Bases
body: **Step 1:** Arrhenius: a base produces OH⁻ ions in water (NaOH → Na⁺ + OH⁻); a soluble base is called an alkali.
**Step 2:** Brønsted–Lowry: a base is a proton (H⁺) acceptor: NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.
**Step 3:** Properties: bitter taste, slippery feel, turn red litmus blue, phenolphthalein pink, pH above 7.
**Step 4:** Bases neutralize acids to form salt and water: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O; with ammonium salts they release ammonia gas.
**Step 5:** Strong bases ionize completely (NaOH, KOH); weak bases ionize partly (NH₃).
**Example:** Titration: 25.0 mL of NaOH is neutralized by 20.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl. n(HCl) = 0.10 × 0.0200 = 0.0020 mol = n(NaOH) (1 : 1). M(NaOH) = 0.0020 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.080 M.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to the Brønsted-Lowry theory, an acid is defined as a substance that does which of the following?

options.B: Accepts a proton ($$\text{H}^+$$) from another substance.
options.C: Donates a proton ($$\text{H}^+$$) to another substance.
options.D: Reacts with metals to form hydrogen gas.

cards.why:
**Step 1: State the Brønsted-Lowry acid-base definition**
According to Brønsted and Lowry, acid-base reactions involve proton transfer.
*   An acid is a **proton ($$\text{H}^+$$) donor**.
*   A base is a **proton acceptor**.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Therefore, the correct statement is **Donates a proton ($$\text{H}^+$$) to another substance.**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following chemical formulas represents a strong acid?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify strong vs. weak acids**
Strong acids completely dissociate in water, while weak acids only partially dissociate.

**Step 2: Classify options**
*   $$\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$ (acetic) is weak.
*   $$\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$$ (carbonic) is weak.
*   $$\text{HF}$$ (hydrofluoric) is weak.
*   $$\text{HCl}$$ (hydrochloric) is a strong mineral acid.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct strong acid is **$$\text{HCl}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following is a definition of a **Bronsted-Lowry base**?
cards.why:
According to the Bronsted-Lowry theory:
- An **Acid** is a proton ($$ H^+ $$) donor.
- A **Base** is a proton ($$ H^+ $$) acceptor.

**Result:** D

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: A substance that donates a proton is ________ according to________ theory.  A) acid, Arrhenius  B) base, Arrhenius  C) acid, Bronsted and Lowry  D) base Bronsted and Lowry  E) None

steps.text:
**Step 1.** **Step 1: Recall definitions.**
- **Arrhenius:** Acid produces $$ H^+ $$ in water.
- **Bronsted-Lowry:** Acid is a proton ($$ H^+ $$) donor; Base is a proton acceptor.
- **Lewis:** Acid is an electron pair acceptor.

**Result:**
Acid, Bronsted and Lowry.

**Step 1: Define normal and acid salts**
*   Normal salts have all acidic Hydrogen atoms replaced by metal cations.
*   Acid salts retain one or more replaceable Hydrogen atoms in their formulas.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Calculate the pH of an aqueous solution where the hydrogen ion concentration is exactly $$[\text{H}^+] = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M}$$.
cards.why:
**Step 1: Apply the pH formula**
$$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$$

**Step 2: Substitute and solve**
$$\text{pH} = -\log(1.0 \times 10^{-3}) = -(-3) = 3.0$$

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The pH is **$$3.0$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following acids can produce **normal salt** when they react with a base?
cards.why:
A **normal salt** is formed when all the replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid are completely replaced by a metal or ammonium ion. 

- $$ HCl $$ (monoprotic) forms $$ NaCl $$.
- $$ H_2SO_4 $$ (diprotic) forms $$ Na_2SO_4 $$.
- $$ H_2CO_3 $$ (diprotic) forms $$ Na_2CO_3 $$.
- $$ H_3PO_4 $$ (triprotic) forms $$ Na_3PO_4 $$.

Since all these acids can have all their hydrogens replaced, they all produce normal salts.

cards.title: Salts
body: Salt = acid H replaced by a metal/ammonium. Prepare: metal + acid, carbonate + acid, base + acid, precipitation for insolubles.

cards.title: Lab pattern for salts
body: Soluble salt from a metal, base or carbonate: add the solid to warm acid until some remains (acid is used up), filter off the extra solid, evaporate until crystals form, cool, filter, dry. Excess solid method avoids leftover acid in the crystals. Insoluble salt: mix two solutions that swap partners, filter, wash, dry — precipitation.

Titration hygiene: rinse pipette with the solution it will measure, burette with the other, conical flask with distilled water only (you will add a known volume next). Repeat to concordant titres. Indicator choice: strong acid / strong base — almost any; weak acid / strong base — phenolphthalein.
pH is a log scale. Jumping from 4 to 3 is not “a bit more acid” — it is ten times the [H⁺]. Universal indicator is a rainbow estimate; a pH meter is a number.

According to solubility rules:
1. All nitrates ($$ NO_3^- $$) are soluble.
2. All Group 1 (Na, K) and ammonium ($$ NH_4^+ $$) salts are soluble.

cards.title: 4.5.1 Measuring pH
body: Measurement of the pH of a pool is important, because if the pH is not within a certain range, it can cause skin problems or may cause bacteria grow.
A universal indicator that shows a series of colour changes at different pH values, and indicates the acidity or alkalinity of a solution that is under investigation.

cards.title: Step by step: The pH scale
body: **Step 1:** pH measures acidity: pH = −log[H⁺]. The scale runs from 0 to 14 at 25 °C.
**Step 2:** pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral (pure water), pH > 7 basic (alkaline).
**Step 3:** Each unit of pH is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.
**Step 4:** pH + pOH = 14, where pOH = −log[OH⁻].
**Step 5:** Measure pH with universal indicator (colour chart), pH paper or a pH meter (most accurate).
**Example:** [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ M → pH = 3 (acidic). A 0.01 M NaOH solution: [OH⁻] = 10⁻² → pOH = 2 → pH = 14 − 2 = 12 (basic).

cards.title: Mnemonic — "Low pH = Lots of H⁺"
body: L-L.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Remember the scale is logarithmic: a change from pH 2 to pH 5 is a 1000-times (10³) decrease in [H⁺], not 3 times.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct option is **Carbon dioxide gas ($$\text{CO}_2$$)**.

questions.q: Ion an acid donates in water?
questions.answer: H⁺ / H₃O⁺.

similar.q: A weak acid  A) completely dissociates in water solution.  B) contains the highest percentage of hydronium ion.  C) contains a higher concentration of ionized acid molecules.  D) contains the highest number of hydronium ion.  E) slightly dissociates in water solution.
similar.a: E. slightly dissociates in water solution. — Complete dissociation and a high hydronium concentration describe strong acids. Answer: E.

questions.answer: Alkali is a base that dissolves in water.
why: A base neutralises an acid; an alkali is a base that dissolves in water to give OH⁻ ions (NaOH is an alkali, CuO is a base but not an alkali).

similar.a: D. can accept a proton. — NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺: ammonia accepts a proton (its lone pair). 'Forms OH⁻ in water' is the Arrhenius idea, not the Brønsted–Lowry reason. Answer: D.

questions.answer: Fully dissociated, not “very concentrated”.
why: A strong acid ionises completely in water (HCl → H⁺ + Cl⁻); strength is not the same as concentration, which is the amount per volume.

why: Pure water has equal concentrations of H⁺ and OH⁻ (10⁻⁷ mol/dm³ at 25 °C), so its pH is 7 — neutral.

similar.q: Sodium hydroxide is used  A) in alkaline batteries.  B) as a household cleaner.  C) in the manufacture of soap.  D) as an antacid.  E) to purify water.
similar.a: C. in the manufacture of soap. — Alkaline batteries use KOH; antacids use Mg(OH)₂ or Al(OH)₃. NaOH is also found in drain and oven cleaners, so B is true in everyday life.

similar.a: B. citric acid. — Acetic acid – vinegar; lactic acid – sour milk; hydrochloric acid – gastric juice. Answer: B. (Raw grapes contain mainly tartaric and malic acids, but citric acid is the intended answer.)

questions.q: Why rinse a pipette with the solution it will measure?
questions.answer: Stops leftover water diluting your known concentration.
why: Water left in the pipette would dilute the solution and change its concentration; rinsing with the solution itself ensures the measured volume has the correct concentration.

similar.q: When an oxide of an active metal, such as K₂O, CaO, etc., dissolves in water, the resulting solution is  A) acidic.  B) basic.  C) neutral.  D) amphoteric.  E) salty.
similar.a: B. basic. — The hydroxides release OH⁻ ions, so the solution is basic (alkaline). Answer: B.

questions.answer: A
